text:
Spoken by Lesbia.
What certain Hazards do Poor Women run ! They bear, believe, they tast, and are undone ;
As they to Men their yielding Hearts ' resign ,
And think to meet such after-Claps as mine.
Left therefore , the mistaker Sex should plead
Custom from me to venture and succeed ;
And without Hymen ' s leave , too rasbly prove
The Dangers that attend unlawful Love.
Let those whose Breasts of softer Mold are made,
And seem more liable to be betray'd ,
From me these Observations rightly take
That Vertue is esteem'd for Vertue's sake,
And Hands, and Seals, and Oaths cannot secure
A mind like Man ' s unfaithful and impure ,
Tho ' I by chance have gain'd the wish'd for Prize ,
And have my Lover fast in lasting Tyes.
When once possess'd, we like fine Garments shew, That last a while, and are flung by for New, And tho' ten thousand LESBIAS may be seen, Where is that Man alive would att BEAUMINE?

ACT I. SCENEI.
#
Enter Lucilia and Lysetta
Lu. Does the Fool think to threaten me into Love? Hearts must be won a softer way.
Ly. Ay Madam, but our Fear often does the Mens Business as well as our Inclinations; more Women have sacrific'd their Vertue to Reputa tion, than ever Love has ruin'd; and if they can but make us kind', what need they care why we are so?
Lu. Cleon seems indeed to be of that Opinion.
Ly. Every Man is, that would be master of his Pleasure.
Lu. Phillabell has told me a thousand times, he shou'd not think me his, unless my Inclination gave me to him.
Ly. Because he finds that his best Friend, if he wou'd refuse you from any other, it does not much recommend his Love.
Ln. That 's your Notion, but ever since I have begun to know my self, your Maxims are not Oracles with me, you shall no more debauch my Reason.
Ly. Why Madam, what false Maxims did I ever give you?
Lu. Shou'd you not have warn'd me of the Deceit and Treachery of Men? Instead of that, what did you entertain me with, but Tales of happy or unhappy Lovers? All to insinuate the violence of Cleon's Passion; How did you represent him to my vanity, adoring, dying for me? I thought it a fine thing to be courted in Rhimes and Extafies, tho' ev'n in that distinguishing Age he never pleas'd me, which you knew; and therefore to move my pity, made my credulous Ignorance believe, that if I wou'd not give him some hopes, he must infallibly die for me; the poor Innocent thought she was oblig'd in Conscience to save a Man's Life!
Ly. Lord! Madam, what ado is here about nothing! Where was the harm of writing a few kind Letters to a Man? Is there ever a Lady in Paris, that has not done more for half a dozen before she can resolve to Marry one? And a Wife Husband wou'd no more Repine at that, than he wou'd that his Cloaths does not come directly to him from the Weavers; all the little Gallantries do but Fashion her for his wearing.

Beau. Nay, thou hast thought of a way now to put a Man out of his Humor, with a vengeance, but the worst Contrivance to raise an Appe- tite you could have found out; you have all of a Wife, but the Name, the want of that flatters me with an imagin'd Liberty, and you must bring it in, to spoil a Man's Fancy.
Lef. I like your Railery, Beaumine, since I don't doubt but you; serious Thoughts are to make me that in earnest, which the Name of, serves you for a Jeft.
Beau. Ay, ay, there will be a time for serious Thoughts, Respect and Reverence, which Wives should have, and that you know, is paid to Antiquity, Lesbia; but Love and Raptures, for the young and free.
Lesf. Thus, I can never be satisfy'd, or angry with this Man; Is it impossible for you ever to answer seriously and directly, Beaumine?
Beau. Why truly, if you would have my Thoughts, I wou'd counsel you against the most unaccountable Extravagance, you are designing.
Lef. What's that?
Bean. You have now a great deal of my Love, 'tis certain Marriage won't add one Jot to it, and very possible it may extreamly lessen it; Now would any one in their Senses, that were in Possession of a good Estate, without any prospect of bettering it, put it to the Chance of a Dye, whether they should keep it or lose it? I am thy own, and keep me as thou hast me. ( Sings ) Thus ever Frolick, ever gay.
Lef. Thou art the most agreeable, tormenting Devil ; But pri'thee, tell me, what I am to expect.

text:
( 28 )
Bean. But they must be perpetually dangling at one another's Elbows; and the little time they are parted, enquiring after every Action or Step they take, for fear they should go aftray.
Mi. So tire one another when together, and torment themselves affunder; and no wonder, they soon break a knot, that with drawing too strait, fits uneasy upon them, and is the weaker it self, bursts upon the least irregular Motion.
Beau. Well, Madam, that we may profit by others folly's, I believe it's time to part before we are weary of one another.
Mi. For now we have told all our thoughts, we are in great danger of growing dull; next time we meet, ten to one, but we shall be quite of another mind, and so new again; In order to it, I'll give you a Song made by Heroick Lover of mine, perhaps it may infect you with Sighing, Whining, Dying Love. Who's there? Desire the Gentlewoman in the next Room to walk in; you'll oblige us, Madam, with the Song I gave you last to learn. (After a Song.) Well Beaumine, How does it affect you?
Beau. I melt, I languish, am all transport, now, ( Sings a Line of the Song ) What shall I say to work upon thy Soul !
Mi. O most Apish! How ridiculous a Man appears when he would cross Nature! He may as well expect to be finely shaped by putting on another Man's Cloaths, because they fit well upon him they were made for, as to please, by affecting the most agreeable Humour in another, it hangs as awkwardly upon him, and is as easily perceiv'd not to be his own.
Beau. Then I must e'en stay from you till I am so much forgot, my own will be new again.
Mi. Which need not be long, I assure you, out of sight, out of mind. Beau. A pleasant way of inviting me to return soon,
Thus whilst the Artful Sex in words deny,
The secret sense, and their kind looks comply. (Ex. Beau.
Mir. Thus we gain Lovers, and secure our Fame,
We promise nothing, and they nought can Claim.
They fancy Pleasures when we speak of Pain ,
And hopes enough , their Passion to maintain.
Ex. Mir.

Co.1. You knew my Credulous Nature fit to work on, and now I should deserve to be so used, be made the Tool you meant me for, if I again believed; but no, Miranda, I've broke my Chain, and here I throw it from me; Thus from my Injured Heart, I'll throw you too for ever. (Going.
Mi. O come back, I beg you.
Con. Never.
Bon. But, Sir, pray consider, as the Lady was saying, she's a young Lady, and a Rich Lady, and might have any Body she pleaes, I would Marry her with all my Heart, my self, tho' I'm resolved never to Marry, so what need can she have---
Con None of me, Sir, so pray give me leave.
Bon. Nor of any Man for a Tool, Sir, for this I can say, she had no design to have a Gallant, for as soon as the Gentleman talk'd of Love to her, she pro pos'd Marriage.
Con. She was very forward it seems----I must be gone, Sir.
Bon. Forward, Sir.--- Oh, I suppose that.--- Nay, hear me, Sir. ( As he offers Con. Provoking Coxcomb. ( to go, Bon. still stops him.
Lef. This is Barbarous, for shame, Constant, you won't leave her thus in Tears. Con. Tears, come, Madam, you need not hide your Mirth, (Taking her hand I can Laugh with you now, Ha! she weeps indeed! (kerchief from her Face. O let those pretious Drops fall on this Boom, soften this stubborn Heart, that would contend against thy Virtue, and its own Perfwasion.
Bon. Ay, I knew I should Reconcile 'em at last.
Mi. Why will you believe? These Tears, may be dissembled.
Con. No, thou art Truth it self,and my Proud Heart wanted but this excuse for its Submission,; Can you forgive me?

Mi. Indeed you were unkind, tho' you had reason, for, I confess, I have not us'd you well.
Con. Do you confess it? 'Tis too large Attonement; O that in this soft Minute I could hear my Charmer speak me Happy ; Tell me, Miranda, when will you be mine ?
Mi. Indeed the Apprehension of losing you was so dreadful to me; that now, methinks, I can't be secure of you too soon.
Con. Shall it be to Morrow then?
Mi. You Dispose of me.
Con. To Morrow then, Miranda, makes us one; O my Transported Soul leaps at the Thought, as if it would break forth, to speak its Joy! it will not stay, but flys to meet with thine through this lov'd Bosom, and take an Earnest of our coming Blifs.---To Morrow, my Miranda, O my Love!

Gr. Indeed you thant, Sir.
Bon. Try me but once, If I don't make all well again -
Gr. Pray, hold your tongue, Sir.
Bon. Well, I will hold my Tongue then, if you'll let me go, for I know you'll begin a Quarrel now, and put Beaumine out of his good humour, and then he'll never let you go to the Devil in quiet, Cousin O there's my Brothers Rival, I must talk with him, stay for me but a little while now.
Enter Phillabell.
Gr. Little enough, I promise you a lucky deliverance. (Ex. Gr.
Gr. Little enough, I promise you a lucky deliverance. (Ex. Gr. Bon. Sir, your humble Servant happening to see you take up a Letter in the Walks, I imagine it might be one my Brother expected there, because he did not receive it.
Ph. If he wou'd know what it contain'd, no doubt the Lady that sent it will inform him.
Bon. Ay, Sir, but that is not the thing now, I can tell you more, because you have reason to take it ill, to shew you have no reason, Sir.
Pb. No reason, Sir?
Bon. Not a dram, Sir, upon my word, for you must know all the kind things in it, were only to pacify my Brother, for fear he shou'd shew you the rest of her fond Letters, not but she really design'd to Marry you.

text:

Ly. Look you, Madam, take my advice; he's a Lover, and by consequence credulous; that will make him believe you enough to have
a mind to examine me ; and being jealous, he'll probably doubt you enough, to do it immediately that we mayn't have time to lay our Heads together, 'tis very likely he'l come directly from you, to look
for me, then let me alone for the rest of the project. I engage to return
him to you, the most Satisfy'd, humble thing, begging pardon, calling
himself a jealous pated Coxcomb, and you the most innocent injur'd Enter. a young Woman, Servant of Lucilias, Neice to Lyfetta.

Lu. Well, well, be gone, I hear him.

Lys. I beg your Pardon, Madam, I did not think any harm wou'd come on't, but truly I did write some Letters in your Name to Cleon; indeed I did not intend to do you any injury by it.
Lu. No injury! What else could induce you to it? Who fet you on? Ly. Nobody fet me on, but Cleon took care to pay me so well for deceiving him, that I thought it worth my pains.
Lu. It seems Phillabel, you have great Power with her, to make her confess all this.
Bo. What is she Jealous of her? Oh, Madam, there's nothing in that but Money too; he has only given her Money enough, take my word for it.
zu. So I imagine, Sir.
Bo. Pfha, you think 'twas upon some slippery account now, but 'twas only to make her own this Cheat, I can answer for him.
Pb. Prithee give me leave to vindicatemy self, Bonfot.
Bo. With all my heart Sir, now I have satisfied her as to the main point.
Lesf. Ay, like all other Universal Friends, commanding every one alike, their Praifes always injure.
Ph. I took her in the very fact, Madam, my good Genius led me thither just as she was writing, and so intent upon her Treachery, I came into the Chamber unperceive'd, heard her, admiring with her Niece her Skill in counterfeiting your hand so perfectly; when I had heard enough, I snatch'd the Paper, which was to the same effect of that I shew'd you, it having miscarry'd, she was writing it again, which left her no room to deny her guilt, nor me to doubt your innocence.
Lu. 'Twas happy, since it proves a means of putting an end to this Cheat, and gives us power to punish the Author of it, which she shall find severely.
Ph. But first, Lucilia, let us think of our own happiness, that no new chance may cross it.

Gr. I must submit, but may have still I hope, some presence to your Friendship. You have deserved it Sir, and are welcome to share with us this Days Diversions.

Con. I have ordered some Muliqk with your leave, Madam, we'll em-ploy 'em.
Ph. 'Tis time now to think upon the ceremony that yet remains to make us Maker of our wishes.
Beau. Which perform'd, I resolve to shew those Marry'd Men, whom I have laugh'd out of the fondness, or civility, for their Wives, that I have learn'd by their weakness, how to avoid giving 'em a Revenge, and will so shamelessly boast of loving mine, that 'twill put railery out of countenance; and by preserving my complaisance for her, shew I know how to value my self.
For treating them with rudeness, or neglect, Does most dishonour, on our selves reflect; If that respect which their own Merit drew, We think, by their becoming ours, less due : And as in chusing,we their worth approve, We tax our Judgment, when we cease to love.
